opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, this is something I spent a lot of time thinking about, and I think the one-for-one framing is where a lot of robotics companies get into trouble.

If your pitch is "this robot replaces one person," you've capped your value at that person's fully loaded cost. Then you have to subtract everything the robot actually costs: the hardware amortized over its realistic lifetime, not the optimistic one; maintenance; field service; the remote operators who handle edge cases; software updates; and the customer's own time spent integrating it and babysitting it in the early months. Once you add all that up, the margin between "cost of a person" and "cost of a robot" is usually a lot thinner than the spreadsheet in your seed deck suggested.

And people are incredibly flexible. A security guard, a janitor, a warehouse worker isn't really doing one job. They're doing the core task plus a hundred small things: holding a door, answering a question, noticing that something's off, covering for a coworker. A robot that does 90% of the core task often can't eliminate the role, because someone still has to cover the other 10% plus all that long-tail stuff. So you don't actually take a headcount off the books, and the ROI story falls apart.

The models that work better, I think, are the ones where the robot does something a person couldn't economically do, or where one person can supervise many robots. In security, for example, the interesting thing isn't replacing a guard one for one. It's that a robot can patrol consistently at 3am, log everything, and escalate to a remote human who's watching many sites at once. Now you're selling coverage and leverage rather than headcount replacement, and the economics are much more forgiving, because you're not competing head-to-head with minimum wage on a task humans are already great at.

The other thing I'd stress is the human-in-the-loop ratio. Early on you'll have a lot of remote assistance per robot, and your unit economics depend almost entirely on how fast you can drive that down. If you can go from one operator per robot to one operator per twenty robots, that's the whole business. If you can't, you've just built a very expensive telepresence system.

So my rough heuristic: don't sell "a robot instead of a person." Sell either a capability people can't easily provide, or a force multiplier on the people you already have. One-for-one replacement is the hardest possible bar, because you're competing against the most general-purpose machine there is.

r001.rationale: It says a one-for-one replacement pitch “caps your value at that person's fully loaded cost,” identifying the replaced labor cost as the ceiling on the robot’s value.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I spent a lot of time on before Anthropic, back when I was working on Cobalt and we were building robots for security and facilities work. And the honest answer is that the one-for-one replacement framing is usually the wrong way to think about it, even though it's the framing every investor deck uses.

The naive math looks great. You take a job that pays, say, forty or fifty thousand dollars a year fully loaded, you build a robot that costs a hundred thousand to manufacture, you amortize it over three or four years, and you say, look, we're half the cost of a human. Everybody loves that slide.

The problem is that the human is doing about fifteen different things, and your robot does three of them really well. And the customer doesn't actually get to fire the human until you've covered all fifteen, or at least the ones that matter. So what actually happens is you've added cost rather than replaced it, because now they're paying for the robot and for the person who handles everything the robot can't do, plus someone to babysit the robot when it gets stuck. Your unit economics only work once you hit a coverage threshold, and that threshold is almost always higher than people think when they start.

The second thing is that the long tail of edge cases is where all the cost lives. The first ninety percent of a task is maybe ten percent of the engineering. And in robotics, unlike software, every edge case has a physical cost. You need a field tech, you need spare parts, you need someone to go unstick the thing from a doorway at two in the morning. Those costs don't show up in the bill of materials but they absolutely dominate the real economics.

So the way I'd actually assess it is to ask three questions. One, what is the real service cost per robot per year, including remote operators, field support, and downtime? Not the projected one, the measured one. Two, what fraction of the job does the robot cover, and is that fraction high enough that the customer can actually restructure their labor? And three, what's the utilization? A robot that's idle sixteen hours a day is a very different business than one that runs three shifts. That's part of why warehouses and manufacturing have worked and a lot of consumer or office robotics hasn't. The utilization is just there.

And I'd say the interesting thing happening now is that models are shifting where that coverage threshold sits. The long tail used to require a human in the loop basically forever, and that's starting to change. But the physical side of it, the parts and the field techs and the maintenance, that hasn't gotten cheaper the way inference has. So I'm much more optimistic than I was five years ago, but I still think the winners are going to be the ones who are brutally honest about the service cost rather than the ones with the prettiest BOM slide.

r001.rationale: The response compares robot costs with a human’s annual labor cost, but it does not say that labor cost sets a ceiling on what the robot can be charged for.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is to look at the cost per hour of useful work, rather than the sticker price of the robot. If you’re replacing a person one for one, the value is pretty directly bounded by what that labor costs. Then you have to ask: How much of their job can the robot actually do, and how much human support does it need?

For example, if a robot costs $100,000 and does 2,000 hours of useful work a year, spreading that purchase over five years gets you to $10 an hour before maintenance, integration, or supervision. If you can run it across multiple shifts, that gets much more attractive. But if it spends half its time waiting for somebody to rescue it, the economics go the other way very quickly.

So reliability and utilization are really central. A demo that succeeds most of the time can look amazing, but the business depends on what happens when it fails. Does someone spend thirty seconds resetting it, or does it stop an entire production line? That’s why a constrained, repetitive task can be a much better starting point than trying to replace everything a person does.

r001.rationale: The response says that for a one-for-one replacement, the robot’s value is directly bounded by the cost of the replaced labor.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the useful way to look at it is cost per hour of productive work, rather than the sticker price of the robot. If a robot costs $100,000 and you can run it for several years, potentially across multiple shifts, the hardware cost per hour can be pretty low compared with human labor.

But that calculation only works if it’s actually doing useful work. You have to include maintenance, downtime, deployment, and any human supervision. If somebody has to intervene every few minutes, you haven’t really replaced that labor—you’ve moved it somewhere else.

So I’d ask: How much does the customer currently spend to get this task done, and what does the complete robotic system cost to deliver the same output at the same quality? The interesting threshold is when you can offer a clear return on investment on a task the robot can reliably do today. You don’t need it to do every part of a person’s job for that to be a valuable business.

r001.rationale: The response compares the customer’s current labor spending with the complete robotic system cost and seeks a clear ROI, but it does not clearly identify human labor cost as a ceiling on what can be charged for the robot.
